docs.title: Professional Summary
docs.text: Hands-on Technical Leader and Solutions Architect with 15+ years of enterprise platform leadership spanning bare-metal compute, private cloud infrastructure, and federal compliance, alongside over a decade designing competitive robotic systems and authoring real-time Python software controlling swerve drive kinematics, articulated mechanisms, and vision targeting. A practical problem-solver who understands systems from the ground up, verifies data directly at the source, and approaches platforms with rigorous testing and automation discipline—from foundational software QA leadership and enterprise cloud orchestration testing to Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) subsystem validation and tournament diagnostics. Proven track record of entering unfamiliar technical ecosystems, rapidly deconstructing complex architectures, and translating intricate enterprise and federal requirements (FedRAMP / STIGs) into reliable, automated platforms. Demonstrated leadership directing enterprise zero-day incident response across 6,000+ nodes to defend FedRAMP ATO with the HHS PMO, building custom vulnerability data platforms, and serving as the technical bridge across multidisciplinary software, networking, and platform teams.

  • Federal ATO Governance & Enterprise Log4j Response (HHS PMO): Played an integral technical role in the enterprise Log4j response affecting 6,000+ operational bare-metal and cloud systems under the HHS PMO’s FedRAMP ATO governance. docs.title: From Bare Metal to vLLM: Architecting an OpenShift AI Infrastructure Lab from First Principles
docs.text:
In the current industry conversation around Artificial Intelligence, the spotlight is almost exclusively focused on high-level models, prompt engineering, and Python frameworks.

However, in enterprise infrastructure engineering, the reality is very different: AI infrastructure is a bare-metal, storage latency, and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) problem in disguise.

When models fail to serve, clusters lose quorum, or inference latencies spike, the root cause is rarely the neural network code. It is almost always found in the underlying physical and systems primitives: - A PCIe bus lockup or driver crash that panics the kernel. - An IOMMU grouping conflict that leaks DMA between devices. - High etcd disk fsync latency that triggers a Kubernetes control-plane election loop. - Memory fragmentation in GPU VRAM (KV cache) causing out-of-memory cascades. - Host kernel mutex deadlocks during dynamic PCIe accelerator rebinding.

To explore these technologies deeply and apply my deep foundational background in bare-metal compute, hypervisors, and distributed systems to modern accelerator stacks, I designed and built an enterprise-grade AI infrastructure testbed from scratch.

Here is the architectural breakdown of how I designed it, why I made specific trade-offs, and what I learned along the way.

docs.title: 1. Architectural Separation of Concerns: Why Two Repositories?
docs.text:
When setting up a private lab for modern containerized AI workloads, the easiest shortcut is to throw everything into a single monolithic repository: hypervisor configs, cluster provisioning scripts, Kubernetes manifests, and application code.

I deliberately rejected that approach. In production, platform infrastructure and application workloads have fundamentally different lifecycles, blast radiuses, and ownership models.

I split the architecture into two strictly decoupled repositories:

flowchart TD
    subgraph SubstrateRepo["Repository 1: openshift-sno-lab"]
        TF["OpenTofu (KVM / Libvirt)"]
        NET["Isolated virbr-ocp Network<br>(Split-DNS / HAProxy Bastion)"]
        NVME["NVMe Storage Pool<br>(Direct I/O: cache=none, io=threads)"]
        SNO["Red Hat Single-Node OpenShift<br>(RHCOS 4.16+ Control Plane)"]
        TF --> NET
        TF --> NVME
        NET --> SNO
        NVME --> SNO
    end

    subgraph WorkloadRepo["Repository 2: openshift-ai-infrastructure"]
        VFIO["PCIe VFIO State Machine<br>(gpu-host-admin.py)"]
        OP["NVIDIA GPU Operator<br>(ClusterPolicy + CRI-O CDI)"]
        TS["Time-Slicing ConfigMap<br>(1 GPU -> 4 Virtual Slices)"]
        VLLM["vLLM Serving Engine<br>(PagedAttention / Continuous Batching)"]
        SRE["SRE Observability & Runbooks<br>(DCGM, PCIe Bus Reset, Post-Mortems)"]

        VFIO --> OP
        OP --> TS
        TS --> VLLM
        VLLM --> SRE
    end

    SNO ==>|"Provides Declarative K8s API"| OP
  1. openshift-sno-lab: Declarative Platform Substrate Responsible solely for provisioning the Single-Node OpenShift (SNO 4.16+) hypervisor substrate on bare-metal Dell Precision workstation hardware via OpenTofu and KVM/libvirt. It guarantees zero host collision, isolated networking, NVMe storage performance, and zero-trust cryptographic SSH key pinning.
  2. openshift-ai-infrastructure: Accelerator & Workload Layer Consumes the Kubernetes API provided by the substrate. It is responsible for host PCIe VFIO driver binding, deploying the NVIDIA GPU Operator, configuring GPU time-slicing, orchestrating production vLLM inference serving, and codifying Day-2 SRE operational runbooks.

By enforcing this boundary, the OpenShift cluster can be upgraded, torn down, or re-initialized without touching the AI workload configs, and model serving deployments can iterate rapidly without risking hypervisor stability.

docs.title: 2. Taming the Physical Substrate: PCIe VFIO & etcd Storage Latency
docs.text: A container platform is only as reliable as the bare metal underneath it. Two critical physical constraints had to be solved before a single container could be scheduled:

docs.title: Guaranteeing etcd fsync Latency (<10ms)
docs.text:
Kubernetes relies on etcd as its distributed key-value store. If disk write latency (fsync) exceeds 10 milliseconds (p99), etcd members miss heartbeats, trigger election storms, and the cluster enters an unrecoverable crash loop.

When virtualizing Single-Node OpenShift on KVM, host filesystem caching introduces unpredictable I/O jitter. To satisfy the <10ms requirement deterministically: * Dedicated an NVMe PCIe adapter pool (/mnt/nvme_data). * Configured KVM Libvirt disk domain overrides using Direct I/O (cache=none) to bypass the host page cache entirely. * Configured dedicated I/O threads (io=threads) to isolate disk writes from hypervisor CPU contention.

docs.title: Host PCIe VFIO Binding & IOMMU Grouping
docs.text:
To provide bare-metal CUDA compute to containers inside OpenShift, the physical NVIDIA GPU on the host had to be passed through cleanly.

Normally, the host Linux kernel automatically binds its nvidia or nouveau driver to the GPU. To hand control over to the virtualized cluster: * I wrote an automated Python state machine (gpu-host-admin.py) that audits sysfs (/sys/bus/pci/devices/). * Verified that the GPU and its onboard HDMI audio controller shared an isolated IOMMU group so Direct Memory Access (DMA) transactions would not bleed across devices. * Executed dynamic unbinding from host drivers and bound the card to the kernel's vfio-pci driver prior to VM initialization.

docs.title: 3. Cloud-Native Accelerator Management: The GPU Operator & CDI
docs.text:
In legacy environments, exposing a GPU to a container required vendor-specific runtime wrappers (such as nvidia-docker or patching Docker daemons with nvidia-container-runtime).

In a modern enterprise OpenShift cluster, that approach is an operational anti-pattern. Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) is an immutable operating system—the root filesystem is read-only, and you cannot SSH in to manually install driver packages.

I leveraged the NVIDIA GPU Operator with the modern Container Device Interface (CDI):

flowchart LR
    subgraph OperatorControl["OpenShift Control Plane"]
        CP["ClusterPolicy Custom Resource"]
        OP["GPU Operator Controller"]
        CP --> OP
    end

    subgraph NodeStack["RHCOS Worker Node"]
        CRIO["CRI-O Container Runtime"]
        CDI["CDI Specification (/var/run/cdi)"]
        DRV["Driver Container (Kernel Module Injection)"]
        PLUGIN["NVIDIA K8s Device Plugin"]
        DCGM["DCGM Exporter DaemonSet"]

        OP --> DRV
        OP --> PLUGIN
        OP --> DCGM
        DRV --> CDI
        CDI --> CRIO
    end

    subgraph Pods["Workload Pods"]
        VLLM["vLLM Inference Engine<br>(resources: nvidia.com/gpu: 1)"]
        CRIO --> VLLM
    end

docs.title: Why CDI (Container Device Interface) Matters
docs.text: CDI is an open standard that allows container runtimes (CRI-O, containerd) to interact with complex third-party hardware without vendor-specific runtime hacks. The GPU Operator injects declarative CDI JSON specifications into /var/run/cdi, describing the exact device nodes and capabilities. When a pod requests nvidia.com/gpu, CRI-O uses standard Linux cgroups and mount namespaces to expose the card safely.

docs.title: Multiplexing Accelerators via Time-Slicing
docs.text:
Datacenter GPUs (like NVIDIA A100/H100) support Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) for hardware-level memory partitioning. On workstation GPUs (like the RTX 3060), running separate small inference tasks requires software multiplexing.

I configured the NVIDIA Device Plugin via a declarative ConfigMap for time-slicing: 

version: v1
sharing:
  timeSlicing:
    resources:
      - name: nvidia.com/gpu
        replicas: 4
This divides 1 physical GPU into 4 virtual slices, allowing concurrent test pods and health monitors to schedule against accelerator resources without starving each other.

docs.title: 4. High-Throughput Model Serving: vLLM, Continuous Batching & PagedAttention
docs.text: Once hardware acceleration was operational inside OpenShift, I deployed vLLM as an enterprise OpenAI-compatible inference engine (serving models such as Qwen 2.5 and Llama 3.1).

docs.title: The Memory Problem: KV Cache Fragmentation
docs.text:
In transformer-based LLMs, generating text requires caching intermediate key-value attention tensors (the "KV Cache") for every prior token in the sequence.

Traditional inference servers allocate large, contiguous VRAM buffers based on the maximum possible context length (e.g., 8,192 tokens). This leads to massive memory waste: * Internal fragmentation: Memory reserved for tokens that were never generated. * Over-allocation: Memory locked up by waiting requests, leading to premature Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors.

docs.title: The Solution: PagedAttention
docs.text: vLLM resolves this by borrowing one of the most fundamental concepts from OS kernel design: virtual memory paging. Instead of allocating contiguous physical GPU memory, PagedAttention breaks the KV Cache into small blocks (pages) stored in non-contiguous VRAM. The attention layer translates virtual token positions to physical memory blocks dynamically, slashing memory waste to nearly 0% and doubling the concurrent request capacity of the GPU.

docs.title: Continuous Batching
docs.text: Rather than using static batching (where an entire batch of user queries must finish before the next batch starts), vLLM implements continuous (iteration-level) batching. As soon as one query outputs an <end-of-sequence> token, its memory pages are immediately freed, and a new incoming query is slotted into the active GPU execution loop on the very next token step.

docs.title: 5. SRE in Practice: Diagnosing Kernel Deadlocks & PCIe Bus Recovery
docs.text: The defining mark of Site Reliability Engineering is how you handle unexpected hardware failures and operational toil. Two real-world incidents in this testbed highlight the difference between superficial administration and first-principles SRE:

docs.title: Incident 1: The Hypervisor Kernel Deadlock & Workload Scheduling Post-Mortem
docs.text:
During initial accelerator lifecycle automation and model bring-up, the physical workstation host froze: the network card still responded to ICMP pings, but SSH sessions, systemd D-Bus RPCs, and terminal sessions hung indefinitely, requiring a manual hardware power cycle.

Rather than dismissing it as a random glitch, I initiated a formal SRE Root Cause Analysis (Incident 001 Post-Mortem): 1. The Investigation: Inspected lingering process telemetry and /proc/<pid>/wchan. Identified worker processes (modprobe nvidia-drm and sb_admin.py) trapped in TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE (D state) blocked on down_console_sem. 2. The Root Cause: An AB-BA mutex race occurred between sysfs virtual console unbinding (/sys/class/vtconsole/vtcon*/bind) and dynamic DRM driver initialization, locking console_lock. Because processes in D state ignore signals, systemd PID 1 console workers froze. Concurrently upon recovery, PyTorch Inductor spun up 32 unvectorized compilation threads across dual legacy Xeon CPUs lacking AVX2, and Kubernetes' default RollingUpdate deadlocked waiting for the single exclusive GPU (nvidia.com/gpu: 1) to release. 3. The SRE Resolution: Sanitized the host prep script to eliminate hazardous vtconsole manipulation, injected --enforce-eager to bypass Inductor JIT on legacy CPUs (slashing startup CPU load from 3200% aggregate to <12% and stabilizing model initialization to 14s), and declared strategy: { type: Recreate } in Kubernetes manifests. Enforced all rules through automated CI unit test guardrails.

docs.title: Incident 2: Automated PCIe Bus Reset vs. Node Reboots
docs.text:
When an accelerator hangs or throws an Xid error under corrupted memory or driver panics, the naive operational response is to reboot the physical host. In a multi-tenant cluster, rebooting a physical node evacuates all healthy workloads and causes significant service disruption.

I authored an automated operational runbook (gpu-recovery.md) utilizing the Linux kernel sysfs reset interface: 

# Gracefully drain GPU pods from the node
oc adm drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# Force hardware reset directly across the PCIe bus without rebooting the host
echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:03:00.0/reset

# Rebind driver and uncordon node
oc adm uncordon <node-name>
This recovers degraded accelerator silicon in under 15 seconds with zero disruption to the hypervisor or neighbor workloads.

docs.title: 6. Conclusion: Bridging 30 Years of Systems Engineering to the AI Era
docs.text:
Mastering modern cloud-native AI platforms doesn't require abandoning decades of foundational systems engineering. In fact, the opposite is true: the engineers who understand bare-metal compute, PCIe buses, storage latency, and kernel drivers are uniquely positioned to make AI infrastructure truly reliable.

By building this testbed from first principles, I was able to validate: - How declarative GitOps and OpenTofu enforce clean separation of concerns. - How immutable OS environments like RHCOS handle low-level kernel drivers and hugepages via MachineConfigs. - How modern serving runtimes like vLLM optimize memory hierarchies through PagedAttention. - How SRE discipline—from automated recovery runbooks to blameless post-mortems—turns fragile bleeding-edge technology into resilient enterprise platforms.

Whether managing 6,000 nodes of enterprise cloud compute or optimizing high-throughput GPU supercomputing clusters, the core principles remain unchanged: understand the systems from the silicon up, automate deterministically, and engineer for failure resilience.

docs.title: Scaling Continuous Compliance with SRE Error Budgets: Protecting 6,000+ Multi-Cloud Federal Systems
docs.text:
When I first joined Cisco Webex as a contractor, vulnerability management felt completely reactive.

My manager would periodically hand me a list of critical security vulnerabilities that needed to be patched across our infrastructure. Every time a new list landed on my desk, I felt like I was getting blindsided—constantly putting out fires instead of getting out ahead of the work.

I wanted to be proactive, so I asked for direct access to our Jira instance so I could see vulnerabilities the moment they showed up and patch them immediately. But once I got inside, I ran straight into three major roadblocks:

  1. The Isolated Federal Boundary: Our Jira instance lived strictly inside our isolated FedRAMP boundary. Almost nobody on the other engineering teams ever logged into it, which meant my manager and I were practically the only ones looking at the data. Other engineers quickly started coming to me just to ask what was open on their systems.
  2. Missing Enterprise Tooling: The company hadn't licensed any of the enterprise portfolio management plugins or advanced add-ons needed to manage compliance tickets at scale.
  3. The "1-Host, 1-Ticket" Deluge: The upstream automation connecting our Qualys scanner to Jira created a separate ticket for every single host affected by a CVE. If I had a cluster of 100 VMware ESXi hypervisors that needed the same routine kernel patch, I had 100 individual Jira tickets to track, update, and close.

I didn't have administrative access to change how Qualys ran or rewrite the upstream ticketing automation. I just had a painful, broken process that was eating up engineering hours.

So I decided to build my own solution.

docs.title: 1. The Genesis: Inverting the Problem with Python and PostgreSQL
docs.text:
I started by using the Jira REST API to pull all open tickets past the boundary barrier and into a PostgreSQL database I designed from scratch.

Once the data lived in a real relational database, I could flip the architecture upside down:

graph TD
    subgraph LegacyProblem["The Upstream Bottleneck: 1-to-1 Multiplication"]

docs.title: 3. The Vulnerability Error Budget: Partnering with the Director of Security
docs.text:
Later, our compliance team moved into the Security Group under our Director of Security.

That move brought us face-to-face with an industry-wide dilemma: how do you balance strict security compliance deadlines against engineering feature delivery?

In traditional compliance, the world is binary: you are either 100% compliant or you are failing. This creates constant friction. Security teams demand that engineering stop everything to patch a low-risk bug, while product teams push back to hit customer release dates.

Our Security Director needed an objective way to quantify risk and report monthly compliance posture to executive leadership. He wanted to define an acceptable risk spend for each engineering domain—an SRE-style Error Budget applied to vulnerabilities.

He determined the policy—what the monthly risk budget should be for each team—and I designed and coded the mathematical algorithms to calculate that spend.

flowchart TD
    subgraph "1. Issue Stream"
        V[("Active Federal Compliance Findings")]
    end

    subgraph "2. The Risk Calculation Engine"
        V --> T["Time Decay Vector (Δt)<br/>Statutory SLA - Days Open"]
        V --> B["Fleet Blast Radius (N_hosts)<br/>COUNT(DISTINCT affected_hosts)"]
        V --> C{"Variance Check<br/>Operational Requirement (OR)?<br/>Vendor Dependency (VD)?"}

        C -- "Approved Exception" --> Credit["Variance Credit Granted<br/>Exempted from Burn Spend"]
        C -- "No" --> Calc["Active Burn Spend<br/>Risk = Weight(Severity) × N_hosts × Decay(Δt)"]
    end

    subgraph "3. Closed-Loop Governance"
        Calc --> CostView[("VIEW: current_poams_vuln_cost_by_poam")]
        Credit --> CostView
        CostView --> Dash["Risk Envelope Scatter Plot<br/>(X: Days Left | Y: Blast Radius)"]
        CostView --> Heatmap["Weekly Monday Trend Matrix<br/>(Green: Clean → Red: Budget Blown)"]
        CostView --> TabPy["Executive Tableau Scorecards"]
        Heatmap --> Decision{"Director Governance<br/>Budget Exceeded?"}
        Decision -- "Yes" --> Freeze["Sprint Reallocation:<br/>Pause Features → Remediate Backlog"]
        Decision -- "No" --> Ship["Maintain Normal Sprint Velocity"]
    end

docs.title: 4. How the Error Budget Algorithm Worked
docs.text: I built the algorithm around four practical principles:

docs.title: 1. The Time Decay Vector ($\Delta t$)
docs.text: Every vulnerability was measured directly against its statutory FedRAMP deadline: $$\Delta t = \text{Scheduled Completion Date} - \text{Current Evaluation Date}$$ * High Severity: Statutory 30-day window. * Moderate Severity: Statutory 90-day window. * Low Severity: Statutory 180-day window. * When $\Delta t \ge 0$, the team was within their allowed buffer. When $\Delta t < 0$, the issue entered a Delayed state, directly burning the team's monthly error budget by $|\Delta t|$ overdue days.

docs.title: 2. Fleet Blast Radius ($N_{\text{hosts}}$)
docs.text: We didn't treat a vulnerability on one isolated test server the same as a vulnerability exposed across 100 core production hypervisors. The algorithm factored in exposure: $$\text{Blast Radius} = \text{COUNT}(\text{DISTINCT } \text{host})$$ In our Dash application, this formed the Risk Envelope: * X-Axis: Days left in SLA ($\Delta t$, where zero was the breach line and negative values were overdue debt). * Y-Axis: Number of affected hosts ($N_{\text{hosts}}$). * Any dot in the upper-left quadrant (high host count + overdue SLA) was an immediate visual alarm of a critical budget breach.

docs.title: 3. The Variance Credit Engine (Eliminating Alert Fatigue)
docs.text:
Nothing frustrates engineering teams more than being penalized for delays they cannot control—like waiting on an upstream vendor patch from a virtualization provider or firmware manufacturer.

To eliminate alert fatigue and keep our metrics honest, I built an automated Variance Credit system into our database logic. If an open issue had an approved operational justification, it was tagged with an exception status rather than burning the team's error budget: * Vendor Dependency: The fix was actively blocked waiting on an upstream third-party vendor patch or firmware update. * Operational Requirement: The configuration was a documented architectural necessity formally approved for platform functionality. * Assessment Finding (SAR): An approved milestone tracked under a formal security assessment plan.

In PostgreSQL, our operational cost views checked for these variances first, filtering credited issues out of the active error budget burn: 

WHERE NOT (sla_status IN ('Operational Requirement', 'Vendor Dependency'))
If a team was legitimately waiting on a vendor, their operational budget wasn't docked. This eliminated false alarms, prevented alert fatigue, and built immense trust between our engineering teams and leadership.

docs.title: 4. Closed-Loop Executive Action
docs.text:
• We joined domain service owners directly to their responsible Director in PostgreSQL.
  • I deployed TabPy (Tableau Python Server) to expose live Python calculations and Postgres views directly to corporate Tableau Server dashboards, giving our Security Director one-click visibility for monthly executive readouts.
  • If a domain exhausted its error budget, leadership stepped in with clear guidance: non-critical feature work was temporarily paused, and sprint capacity was redirected to clearing the compliance backlog until the budget recovered.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Decisions & Trade-Offs
docs.text:
When building systems that process data under continuous production use, architectural trade-offs matter:

Decision What I Chose What I Rejected Why SLA Calculation Engine PostgreSQL Views & PL/pgSQL Application-level Python / Pandas Pulling large volumes of raw tickets into Python memory to calculate date math created high latency and memory spikes. Moving date math into PostgreSQL views let the relational query planner compute aggregations in milliseconds. Ansible Inventory Generation Dynamic REST JSON Endpoint Static file exports (CSV/YAML) Static host files become stale the moment a single server is patched or rebooted. A live REST endpoint queried the database in real time, guaranteeing playbooks only targeted currently unpatched nodes. Lifecycle Auditing Full Jira Changelog Sync Simple point-in-time snapshots Snapshotting only current state hides where tickets get stuck. Ingesting full changelogs allowed us to calculate exact remediation dwell time and identify process bottlenecks between teams. Exception Handling Codified SQL Variance Logic Manual spreadsheet tracking Tracking vendor dependencies in spreadsheets led to human error and audit friction. Codifying variance logic into SQL ensured real-time exclusion from error budgets while preserving full audit trails for federal assessors.

docs.title: 6. Real-World Production Outcomes
docs.text:
Operating continuously across our multi-cloud federal footprint, the platform delivered measurable, sustained improvements across our engineering organization:

  • 10x Velocity Surge: By eliminating manual coordination and enabling single-command Ansible fleet patching, our organization scaled its monthly remediation throughput by roughly an order of magnitude (over 10x).
  • High-Severity Dwell Time Cut by Over 40%: Critical vulnerabilities that previously lingered near or past statutory deadlines saw their remediation turnaround compressed by more than 40%.
  • Overdue Cloud Backlogs Slashed by Over 90%: In our multi-region AWS cloud environments, active overdue vulnerabilities were driven down by more than 90% within months of rolling out the error budget framework.
  • Sustained Low-Backlog Steady State: In our core bare-metal and virtualization environments, overdue compliance issues dropped by roughly 80% over time, keeping ongoing overdue backlogs consistently in low double digits across an enterprise fleet of 6,000+ operational systems.

docs.title: 7. Connecting These Principles to Modern Cloud-Native Platforms
docs.text:
The fundamental lesson from building this platform is that compliance cannot scale through manual ticketing—it has to be engineered into the platform itself.

Today, as infrastructure shifts from virtual machines toward Kubernetes, containers, and GitOps, the exact same governance principles apply:

graph LR
    subgraph "Infrastructure Governance"
        A1["Vulnerability Scanner"] --> A2["Relational Data Store"]
        A2 --> A3["Error Budget Algorithms"]
        A3 --> A4["Dynamic Automated Patching"]
    end

    subgraph "Modern Cloud-Native Governance"
        B1["Container Vulnerability Scanning"] --> B2["Kubernetes Policy Engine (Kyverno)"]
        B2 --> B3["Continuous Compliance Budgets"]
        B3 --> B4["Declarative GitOps Remediation (UDS / Zarf)"]
    end

    A3 -.->|"Core Philosophy"| B3
    A4 -.->|"Automated Execution"| B4
  1. Policy as Code Instead of Ticket Queues: Instead of spawning a Jira ticket when an insecure container image is detected, Kubernetes admission controllers (Kyverno, Gatekeeper) reject non-compliant workloads at deployment time.
  2. Error Budgets for Security Posture: Development clusters can use defined error budgets for non-critical findings, while production clusters enforce zero-breach policies.
  3. Declarative Remediation: What started as dynamic Ansible inventories querying a PostgreSQL endpoint has evolved into declarative GitOps workflows (such as Defense Unicorns Zarf/UDS), where base container images are continuously patched, rebuilt, and deployed through automated CI/CD pipelines.

By approaching compliance as an SRE and systems engineering problem rather than an administrative checklist, security shifts from an organizational bottleneck into an automated, self-healing platform capability.

docs.title: Directing Technical Execution & Rapid Learning: How I Approach New Platforms and Architect for Resilience
docs.text:
When entering an unfamiliar technology stack, what separates a superficial implementation from an enterprise-grade platform?

Over the past several months, I immersed myself in modern systems and cloud-native technologies: OpenTofu, Talos Linux, eBPF (Cilium), GitOps (ArgoCD), Air-Gapped Delivery (Defense Unicorns Zarf/UDS), Compliance-as-Code (Lula/OSCAL), Red Hat OpenShift (SNO 4.16+), PCIe VFIO GPU Passthrough, NVIDIA GPU Operator (CDI), and high-throughput vLLM model serving.

I didn’t just follow "getting started" guides. I built complete, verifiable, self-healing platforms from first principles.

Here is a look into how I learn, how I make architectural decisions, and how I direct technical execution.

docs.title: 1. How I Learn: First-Principles Mental Models & Rapid Prototyping
docs.text:
When approaching a brand-new tool or paradigm, I follow a disciplined 4-step framework:

  1. Deconstruct the Invariants: Strip away the marketing hype to understand the underlying mechanics (e.g., how eBPF kernel hooks bypass iptables, or how OSCAL validates JSON schemas against Kubernetes API endpoints).
  2. Author Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) First: Before writing complex code, I document the context, alternatives considered, trade-offs, and failure modes. Across my projects, you'll find over 30 ADRs governing everything from IPAM schemes to deterministic cryptographic keys.
  3. Build an Isolated Sandboxing Substrate: I construct layered local sandboxes (using KVM/Libvirt and OpenTofu) that faithfully reproduce cloud topologies (isolated subnets, jump hosts, dual NICs) without incurring cloud costs or polluting the host.
  4. Iterate with Rapid Feedback Loops: I build automated preflight checks (doctor.py) and stage verification test harnesses from day one.

docs.title: 2. Directing Technical Execution: Spotting Anti-Patterns & Enforcing Modular Clean Code
docs.text:
Using AI coding assistants provides incredible implementation speed—but speed without architectural discipline creates technical debt at an alarming rate.

As the technical lead in these projects, I actively steer the architecture:

docs.title: Example: Eliminating Script Sprawl with common.py
docs.text:
During the rollout of multi-stage cluster verification, multiple Python scripts were generated with duplicate functions for querying virsh, resolving DHCP MAC leases, checking TCP ports over SSH tunnels, and parsing Terraform JSON outputs.

I halted the sprawl and directed a full refactoring: - Created a unified scripts/common.py library for environment discovery and socket diagnostics. - Engineered a reusable TestReporter class to standardize test recording and ANSI-formatted console feedback across the platform. - Wrote dedicated unit tests (test_common.py) to guarantee reliability.

docs.title: Example: Refactoring Robotics Controls into FROGlib
docs.text: I applied this exact same engineering rigor to FIRST Robotics. When maintaining robot code across competitive seasons, I extracted shared swerve kinematics, AprilTag vision tracking, and motor controller wrappers into FROGlib—an installable Python package with formal pyproject.toml dependency management.

docs.title: Example: Enforcing Separation of Concerns Across Infrastructure Repositories
docs.text:
When exploring enterprise OpenShift and AI infrastructure, the initial temptation is often to dump hypervisor provisioning, kernel drivers, cluster setup, and model workloads into a single monolithic repo.

I rejected that anti-pattern and architected a strict separation of concerns: - openshift-sno-lab handles the declarative platform substrate: OpenTofu, KVM/libvirt, isolated networking (virbr-ocp), and NVMe storage latency tuning (<10ms etcd fsync). - openshift-ai-infrastructure handles the accelerator and workload plane: host PCIe VFIO binding, the NVIDIA GPU Operator (CDI), and OpenAI-compatible vLLM inference serving.

By isolating the substrate lifecycle from the workload lifecycle, either layer can be upgraded, tested, or rebuilt without destabilizing the other.

docs.title: 3. Principles That Guide My Design Decisions
1. Zero Trust & Cryptographic Determinism Over Convenient Shortcuts
docs.text: Never disable security to make automation work. Rather than using -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no to ignore SSH key changes on rebuilt VMs, I engineered deterministic host key generation and injected public keys into Cloud-Init, maintaining 100% strict verification. This pushes security left so we don't have to rely on reactive security patching after the fact.

docs.title: 2. Immutability Eliminates Drift
docs.text: General-purpose Linux on cluster nodes invites interactive SSH tweaks and silent configuration drift. Transitioning to Talos Linux gave us a headless, read-only rootfs with zero SSH daemons and declarative, API-managed machine configs.

docs.title: 3. Compliance Must Be Executable Code, Not Static Paperwork
docs.text: Security compliance shouldn't be an annual scramble with spreadsheets. I implemented continuous compliance using Lula and OSCAL, validating NIST and DoD IL5 controls live against cluster state and automatically generating System Security Plans (SSPs) and SARs.

docs.title: 4. Failure Modes Must Be Engineered and Practiced
docs.text: A platform is only reliable if its failure modes are understood and tested. I designed automated fault-injection scripts simulating etcd split-brain, BGP routing loss, and storage quorum degradation. When operating physical accelerators, I authored Day-2 runbooks to reset hung GPUs over the PCIe bus (/sys/bus/pci/devices/.../reset) without rebooting physical hosts, backed by blameless root-cause post-mortems analyzing kernel mutex deadlocks during dynamic driver rebinding and GPU scheduling contention.

docs.title: Summary: How I Think and Operate
docs.text: Whether working in enterprise backend services, modern Kubernetes platform engineering, or real-time robotics systems, my approach remains constant: - Understand deeply from the ground up. - Enforce architectural integrity and clean, DRY code. - Design for immutability, zero-trust, and failure resilience. - Move fast by leading AI tools with clear direction, not by accepting low-quality shortcuts.
